title: Why Norges Bank held at 4.5% despite stronger domestic inflation
summary: Norges Bank kept its policy rate at 4.5% on 4 November, following September’s increase. The announcement on 5 November explains why the Committee could hold despite an upside surprise in domestic prices. Inflation overall had followed the September projection closely, the krone was stronger than assumed and the economy appeared to be operating slightly below normal capacity. The Committee still expected to need an elevated rate for some time. A further hike remained an option if the inflation outlook warranted it.

September consumer prices were 3.4% above a year earlier. CPI-ATE, which adjusts for tax changes and excludes energy products, rose 3.0%. The first of the release’s two updates on developments since September identifies a more revealing forecast miss. Prices for domestically produced goods and services had risen faster than projected. Firms had faced rapid cost increases over several years, and the Committee thought these would keep upward pressure on prices. It also saw a risk that above-target inflation would become more persistent the longer it lasted. The statement provides no separate reading for household expectations or firms’ pricing plans.

The same update shows why it would be premature to conclude that external pressure was easing. Spot oil fell while oil futures edged up. Both current and forward prices for gas and electricity rose amid continued uncertainty from the conflicts in the Middle East. The Bank’s indicators of overseas pressure on imported goods also moved higher, as it had expected. A stronger krone could cushion the price paid by Norwegian buyers. The release gives neither an estimate of that effect nor the actual contribution of imported items to the inflation surprise. The size and timing of any offset to domestic costs therefore remain open.

The second update separates the level of activity from news about employment. Unemployment had changed little on both the survey and registered measures. Registered unemployment was slightly lower than forecast, and preliminary salaried employment had grown slightly more than expected. These modest surprises were compatible with an economy already running below normal capacity. They gave the Committee little reason to abandon September’s assessment in either direction. More restraint would have a cost if economic slack proved greater than it appeared. A stronger labour market alongside persistently high domestic prices would make it harder to rely on slack to bring inflation down.

The Committee made no new forecasts in November. Its concluding assessment kept September’s outlook as the benchmark until the decision and new projections due on 17 December. For a holder of Norwegian short-dated debt, the distinction is between how long the existing rate might last and whether another increase will actually be needed. The statement offers reasons to watch both, with no timing or probability attached to a hike.

questions.question: How much of the domestic price surprise was being offset by the stronger krone?
questions.detail: The Committee identifies the surprise in domestic goods and services and the currency appreciation. It gives no offset in percentage points. Use the September Monetary Policy Report as the forecast vintage, then compare the official domestic and imported CPI-ATE components, weights and exchange-rate assumptions. Check monthly moves as well as annual inflation. A widening set of domestic price increases would have different implications for the duration of restraint than a few large, temporary moves.

questions.question: Which energy prices were feeding into costs faced by Norwegian firms?
questions.detail: The conflict left spot oil and forward oil moving in opposite directions, while both gas and electricity measures rose. To judge the pressure on margins or the incentive to raise prices, look for official industrial energy-price statistics, contract repricing dates and Norges Bank business surveys available at the meeting. Compare sectors with different electricity exposure. The relevant cost for a producer renewing a contract may differ materially from the headline oil quote.

questions.question: Did the labour-market surprises primarily affect the expected duration or the expected peak of rates?
questions.detail: Employment was preliminary, registered unemployment surprised modestly and both unemployment measures had been little changed. Compare their subsequent scheduled revisions with the September baseline and employer-reported spare capacity. For the market assessment, compare meeting-dated NOK overnight rates around the 10:00 announcement with rates spanning later decisions. A repricing of a prolonged hold could otherwise be mistaken for new conviction about a December hike.
